tweets.text:
This is correct. The vast majority of enterprise workflows have not actually had agents applied to them in any meaningful way. The economy probably has this deployed < 1% right now.

At best you have a few automated systems in a company that do a single pass of an LLM to make a decision or provide feedback, but very little real “automation”. Some of this is a statement about the adoption rates of technology in enterprises, but the vast majority of it is really just due to the capability of AI itself.

That’s all changing. Now with computer use, long running agents, harness improvements and surrounding infrastructure, we’re finally at a point where we can start to apply agents at more complex workflows. 

We will see self-improving systems that can take any particular workflow goal and improve the execution rates over a volume of instances. And with the emerging form factor of agent swarms, you can just choose to deploy any amount of compute at a problem and agents will off and do the work.

This won’t be about and users prompting agents to complete a specific task for them, but instead the organization reengineering the underlying workflows to take advantage of agents in their processes. This will have a massive impact in finance, life sciences, healthcare, and other information-heavy domains. Lots of opportunity to build and deploy these systems right now.

This is the key stat. The average Fortune 500 customer of Anthropic spends less than .1% of their expenses on Anthropic. 

While that number likely will eventually asymptote somewhere (token prices coming down, and other large enterprise spend areas not going away), there’s no reason it can’t be 10-50X higher than this, reaching a “mere” 1-5% of spend. Which would still be a fraction of what most startups are spending.

Thus, you can see how big of a divide there is between the frontier users of AI and the rest of the world still.

Today, only a microscopically small set of companies are actually using agents for large amounts of background tasks and inside of workflows that aren’t human prompted. This Fortune 500 spend is likely dominated by coding tasks and broad employee productivity use-cases.

But the big jump will come as these enterprises start to rewire their underlying processes for agents, which we’re now in the earliest stages of seeing. Agents processing large amounts of data in the enterprises; swarms doing coding, bio research, cyber, and other large fan out tasks; background workflows executing tasks in processes, and so on. All of these use cases generally are 100X bigger consumers of tokens, and much closer to direct ROI on the spend.

This S-1 gives you a sense of both the strength of the frontier lab business model - even amidst massive competition - and how early we are in the build out of AI.

Good assessment of the on the ground reality for security in most large enterprises right now. The fragmented landscape of the risk surface is only going to get more gnarly, making it even more complex for enterprises to solve.

There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure, data, and code to secure. Most large enterprises can barely keep up with this, let alone smaller startups or most companies outside of tech. 

In many cases enterprises need to work to modernize their tech stacks. Data, in most organizations, is highly fragmented which means you don’t really know the state of risk at any given time. Some systems are open up privileges too broadly, and others are operating primarily via security through obscurity. Lots of upgrading here to do.

Once you can get your data and infra into a better spot, at least you have a chance for agents to help you secure the environment. Agent swarms can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. This capability only emerged in the past few months, and none of it would be possible before we had long running agents and computer use good enough.

This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability. 

But everyone does need to do the hard work of getting the basics right at the start.

We’ll likely have 1,000X more tokens flowing through cyber agents soon than we do today. 

As the surface area of cyber risk increases, at some point soon it will be nearly impossible to keep up with the volume of new risks (we’re essentially already there). Large companies barely had the resources to pull this off before, but the vast majority of companies don’t. 

There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure and code to secure. We’ll have agent swarms that can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. 

This capability only emerged in the past few months. Wouldn’t have been possible before long running agents and computer use were good enough, and models hadn’t been trained on cyber deeply. That’s all changing now.

This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability.

The main thing I wanted to dig into @AnthropicAI's S-1 was the compute contracts..

A few things that stood out (built in conjuction with Opus 5.5):

> At June 30, Anthropic had $265.6B of purchase commitments and $321.4B of leases that hadn’t started. That’s a $587B subtotal, payable over years, including some conditional leases. The latest aggregate total is still blank in the filing.

> The contracts are very different. Google and Amazon require minimum spending regardless of usage. SpaceXAI’s agreements have a potential value of $120.5B, but either party can cancel on 90 days’ notice after initial locked periods end in January and March 2027.

> Anthropic Direct separates chips, buildings, power and operations into different contracts. It lets Anthropic reserve a building early and commit to chips later. It also means one supplier can start billing before the others are ready. Equipment rent can begin before the compute is usable.

> Broadcom’s $42B facility never hands Anthropic cash. Notes settle specific equipment rent bills. The facility excludes each equipment pod’s first quarterly payment and any rent due before it is ready for service. Anthropic has to find a way to fund those payments elsewhere.

> Those notes carry 9% interest, added to the balance quarterly, and can convert at 90% of the trailing 30-day average share price after IPO. New notes issued during specified revenue-breach periods get 13% interest and an 85% conversion price. The share-price measure is volume-weighted.

> That interest sits on top of the equipment lease’s own financing charge, whose rate is confidential. The investor chooses whether to convert the notes. Otherwise, principal and accumulated interest come due in cash.

> Anthropic treats Trainium, TPUs, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as a shared fleet across model development, paying customers and internal use. It doesn’t disclose a fixed physical split between training and inference. The supplier bill can be fixed while the work assigned to the hardware changes.

> Revenue per dollar of total compute and infrastructure expense rose from $0.57 in Q2 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026. Pricing, utilization, technical improvements and when capacity arrives all affect that ratio. It’s a substantial improvement in monetizing the compute base.

> About 80% of H1 revenue was consumption-based. Most compute commitments however run for years. With quarterly releases, this bifurcation between usage and subscription will be interesting to monitor.

I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU.

It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip.

I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms:
① CPU contention
② Cache eviction timing
③ DRAM bandwidth contention 

… across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.)

Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency.

The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.)

Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

tweets.text: https://t.co/0E2zuZ5M3N

struggle together

i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again.

when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.

when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.

many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.

it became like water.

i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.

now we can ask a machine.

i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.

we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.

we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.

there is another side to this.

working with people is uncomfortable.

everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.

it takes a while to find each other.

but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.

you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.

you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.

some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.

i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.

an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.

sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?

i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.

and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.

they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.

is that freedom?

or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?

i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.

maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.

sometimes i want to close the laptop.

sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.

like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.

i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.

music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.
